   CITY OF BEVERLY HILLS

  POLICY AND MANAGEMENT

  MEMORANDUM

TO:  City Council Liaison/Legislative/Lobby Committee

FROM:  Mandy Jiang, Senior Management Analyst

DATE:  December 18, 2025

SUBJECT:  Staff Memorandum - Legislative Bills

ATTACHMENT:  1. Lobbyist Memos for Each Bill

INTRODUCTION
This report provides a snapshot summary of the legislative bills brought forth to the City Council
Liaison Legislative / Lobby Committee for consideration. Included in this summary is any
relevant language from the City’s 2025 Legislative Platform that may provide nexus for
recommending a position. Verbal overview of federal legislation will be provided by David Turch
& Associates and overview of state legislation will be provided by Shaw Yoder Antwih
Schmelzer & Lange (SYASL). The attachment to this report includes memos for each bill
provided by the City’s contract lobbyists detailing bill provisions, author’s intent, and those in
support or opposition.

After discussion of each bill, the Liaisons may recommend the following actions:
1) Oppose; 2) Support; 3) Support if amended; 4) Oppose unless amended; 5) Remain neutral;
6) Provide other direction to City staff. Should the Liaisons recommend the City take a position
on a bill, staff will place the item on a future City Council agenda for concurrence.

DISCUSSION
1. S.2651 – ROAD to Housing Act of 2025 – This bipartisan federal bill takes significant steps
to incentivize growth of the nation’s housing supply, improve housing affordability, and increase
oversight and efficiency of federal regulators and housing programs. With much support from
the US Conference of Mayors, this measure invests directly in cities through flexible new grant
programs tied to housing supply and infrastructure readiness; supports community-driven
zoning and land-use frameworks through HUD guidance, and permanently authorizes funding
programs like Community Development Block Grant – Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR), and
enhances other programs such as HOME and Build More Housing Near Transit. One potential
point of concern is verbiage under Sec. 206 (B), which ties some jurisdictions’ Community
Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding to their housing production, including bonuses for
accelerated homebuilding and a 10% funding reduction for jurisdictions lagging behind the
median housing growth improvement rate for all eligible recipients in a fiscal year.
This bill involves a policy matter may be addressed within the adopted Legislative Platform
language: Support legislation which encourages the use of federal and state incentives for local
government action rather than mandates.

2. S.2293 – Muslim Brotherhood Terrorist Designation Act of 2025 – This federal bill
mandates the Secretary of State to designate and catalog the Muslim Brotherhood (MB)
branches as terrorist groups. Currently, the U.S. has officially listed individual members,
branches (including Hamas), and charities of the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorists, but has not
 designated the organization as a whole. This measure would designate MB branches under all
three U.S. statute and authorities: Congressional designation under the Anti-Terrorism Act of
1987 (ATA), State Department. designation as a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) pursuant
to the Immigration and Nationality Act, and Treasury Department designation as a Specially
Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT) under Executive Order (EO) 13224. By doing so, this would
create an embargo prohibiting Americans from conducting financial transactions on behalf of the
group.
This bill involves a policy matter that is not specifically addressed within the adopted Legislative
Platform language but may be associated with: Support legislation which prioritizes fighting
antisemitism, hate crimes and domestic terrorism.

3. H.R.4397 - Muslim Brotherhood Terrorist Designation Act of 2025 - This federal bill
introduced by the House of Representatives and is the companion bill of S.2293; therefore, the
same Legislative Platform language may apply.

4. H.R.3883 - Muslim Brotherhood is a Terrorist Organization Act of 2025 – This federal bill
simply states “The Secretary of State shall designate the Muslim Brotherhood as a foreign
terrorist organization pursuant to section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C.
1189)”. This bill involves a policy matter that is not specifically addressed within the adopted
Legislative Platform language but may be associated with: Support legislation which prioritizes
fighting antisemitism, hate crimes and domestic terrorism.

5. H.R.1267 - Water Systems PFAS Liability Protection Act – This federal bill exempts public
water agencies from liability under the Comprehensive Environmental Response,
Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980, with respect to releases of PFAS (perfluoroalkyl and
polyfluoroalkyl) substances. It aims to protect water utilities, who are passive receivers of PFAS,
from financial and legal liabilities associated with decades of use of these chemicals in
manufacturing and consumer products.
This bill involves a policy matter that is not specifically addressed within the adopted Legislative
Platform language.

6. Legislative Platform – see separate staff memo and draft platform under agenda item #6.

7. 2025 CHP Report for SB 1079 – This item is requested by a Committee member to speak
on supporting a noise activated pilot program. In 2022, the City adopted a “Support” position on
SB 1079 (Portantino) – Vehicles: sound-activated enforcement devices, which was signed into
law by Governor Newsom. The measure required the California Highway Patrol (CHP) to study
the efficacy of sound-activated enforcement devices by evaluating devices from at least three
different companies, and to determine their ability to capture exhaust noise violations sufficiently
to allow for enforcement action. CHP was to report due back to the California State Legislature
in January 2025. With the report now available, the CHP’s conclusion was that none of the three
devices were deemed suitable as a standalone enforcement tool to be used as the sole basis
for issuing citations for exhaust noise violations.
This bill involves a policy matter that is not specifically addressed within the adopted Legislative
Platform.

TO:  Mandy Jiang, Senior Management Analyst
  City of Beverly Hills

FROM:  Jamie Jones
  Jamie.jones@davidturch.com
  202-543-3744

DATE:  November 12, 2025

RE:  Update on S.2651 – ROAD to Housing Act of 2025

Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee Chairman Tim Scott (R-SC) and Ranking
Member Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) introduced S.2651, the Renewing Opportunity in the American
Dream (ROAD) to Housing Act of 2025, this past July. The bipartisan bill takes significant steps
to boost the nation’s housing supply, improve housing affordability, and increase oversight and
efficiency of federal regulators and housing programs. The Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs
Committee unanimously approved the bill by a vote of 24 to 0 on July 29. The measure was passed
by the full Senate last month as an amendment to S.2296, the National Defense Authorization Act.

According to Representative Mike Flood (R-NE), Chairman of the House Financial Services
Subcommittee on Housing and Insurance, the House is likely to take a more “surgical” approach
to addressing the housing and homelessness crises than the Senate bill. For example, Congressman
Flood, in a speech before the US Chamber of Commerce, mentioned his bill, H.R. 5878, that would
make changes to the HOME Investment Partnership Program at the Department of Housing and
Urban Development. The legislation would expand income eligibility for the housing assistance,
allow funds to be used for infrastructure improvements related to HOME projects and ease some
environmental requirements, among other changes. Representative Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO),
ranking member of the housing subcommittee, co-sponsored the bill.

Flood contrasted the bill with the Senate’s proposal for remaking the HOME program. The fact
that the House is looking to consider its own housing bill ensures that the legislative process will
drag well into next year.

SENATE BILL

The comprehensive Senate measure incorporates part of at least 27 previously introduced pieces
of legislation, 23 of which were introduced with bipartisan sponsors. The bill, moreover, contains
no unfunded mandates or preemptions of local authority; invests directly in cities through flexible
new grant programs tied to housing supply and infrastructure readiness; supports evidence-based,
 community-driven zoning and land-use frameworks through HUD guidance, not top-down
mandates; and permanently authorizes CDBG-DR and enhances programs like HOME and Build
More Housing Near Transit, which are essential tools for local governments.

The USCM supports the legislation and is urging member mayors to contact their House delegation
members urging them to endorse the bill. The USCM, however, has expressed concern regarding
language that ties some localities’ Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding to their
housing production, including bonuses for accelerated homebuilding and small funding reductions
for lagging grantees. USCM letter states: “Our concerns with the legislation are focused on any
potential adjustments to the distribution of CDBG funding – one of Washington’s best bipartisan
success stories, which has been a force in revitalizing low- and moderate-income neighborhoods
across the country and serving the people living in them since 1974. This issue will require
discussion as we go forward.”

The ROAD to Housing Act will:

    Expand and Preserve Housing Supply:
  o Remove regulatory barriers to housing development
  o Increase and preserve existing housing
  o Promote innovative construction methods, including to expand access to modular
  and manufactured housing
  o Addresses neighborhood blight and supports communities recovering from natural
  disasters
    Improve Housing Affordability and Access:
  o Expand access to homeownership
  o Improve housing affordability
  o Promote housing opportunities for veterans
  o Reduce homelessness
  o Reduce appraisal shortages while addressing inaccurate appraisals
    Advance Accountability and Fiscal Responsibility:
  o Ensure taxpayer dollars are used efficiently
  o Promote evidence-based policy solutions
    Improve Oversight and Program Integrity:
  o Strengthen oversight of housing regulators
  o Streamline program coordination
  o Ensure performance, transparency, and accountability across housing programs

Below is a summary of the bill’s key provisions:

Title 1 – Improving Financial Literacy
Sec. 101 – Reforms to Housing Counseling and Financial Literacy Programs
   Allows the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to evaluate the
  performance of housing counseling agencies and counselors, mandate additional training,
  and revoke certifications.
Title 2 – Building More in America
Sec. 201 – Rental Assistance Demonstration Program
     Lifts the Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD) program cap and extends protections
  for tenants in RAD buildings.
Sec. 202 – Increasing Housing in Opportunity Zones
   Allows HUD to prioritize applicants that are based in or primarily serve communities
  designated as Opportunity Zones for any competitive grants relating to housing
  development or preservation.
Sec. 203 – Housing Supply Frameworks Act
   Directs HUD to publish guidelines and best practice frameworks for state and local
  zoning and land-use policies.
Sec. 204 – Whole-Home Repairs Act
   Creates a HUD pilot program to support state and local whole-home repair programs,
  which provide grants and forgivable loans to eligible homeowners and landlords for
  home repairs and modifications.
Sec. 205 – Community Investment and Prosperity Act
   Raises the cap on bank public welfare investments, such as affordable housing and
  community development projects, from 15% to 20%.
Sec. 206 – Build Now Act
   Ties some localities’ Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding to their
  housing production, including bonuses for accelerated homebuilding and small funding
  reductions for lagging grantees.
Sec. 207 – Better Use of Intergovernmental and Local Development (BUILD) Housing Act
   Authorizes HUD to treat certain housing assistance as “special projects” to help simplify
  compliance with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).
   Expands HUD’s authority to delegate certain environmental review responsibilities to
  states, local governments, and tribes.
Sec. 208 – Unlocking Housing Supply Through Streamlined and Modernized Reviews Act*
   Streamlines NEPA review for a broad range of housing-related activities—including
  small-scale construction, rehabilitation, and infill development—by expanding
  categorical exclusions to reduce delays and lower administrative burdens.
Sec. 209 – Innovation Fund
   Creates a $200 million annual competitive grant program for local governments and
  tribes that demonstrate measurable increases in housing supply, incentivizing reforms
  such as streamlined permitting, density bonuses, and zoning changes.
Sec. 210 – Accelerating Home Building Act
   Provides grants to local governments and tribes to select and implement pre-reviewed
  housing designs (such as accessory dwelling units, duplexes, or townhouses) to
  streamline affordable housing construction, with 10% of total funding reserved for rural
  areas and a 5-year window for adoption.
Sec. 211 – Build More Housing Near Transit Act
   Incentivizes applicants for federal transit project funding to adopt pro-housing policies—
  including by-right zoning and reduced parking minimums.
Sec. 212 – Revitalizing Empty Structures into Desirable Environments (RESIDE) Act
   Creates a pilot grant program to help local governments convert vacant commercial or
  industrial buildings into affordable housing, prioritizing economically distressed areas
  and Opportunity Zones, with funding from excess HOME Investment Partnerships
  Program grant allocations.
 Sec. 213 – Housing Affordability Act
   Directs HUD to evaluate, and potentially revise, loan limits for Federal Housing
  Administration (FHA) multifamily mortgage insurance programs to better reflect
  construction costs and demand for housing, with proposed increases in per-unit loan
  limits for walk-up and elevator buildings.
Title 3 – Manufactured Housing for America
Sec. 301 – Housing Supply Expansion Act
   Eliminates the permanent chassis requirement for manufactured homes.
Sec. 302 – Modular Housing Production Act
   Directs HUD to conduct a review of FHA construction financing programs to identify
  barriers for modular housing developers and administrative opportunities to reduce any
  such barriers.
   Authorizes HUD to fund a study on the utility of a standardized code for modular homes.
Sec. 303 – Property Improvement and Manufactured Housing Loan Modernization Act*
   Increases the loan limits of FHA-insured manufactured housing loans, adds the
  construction of accessory dwelling units as an acceptable use for FHA-insured property
  improvement loans, and directs HUD to conduct a study on the cost-effectiveness of off-
  site construction techniques.
Sec. 304 – PRICE Act
   Reauthorizes Preservation and Reinvestment for Community Enhancement (PRICE)
  grants to fund the repair, preservation, and improvement of existing manufactured homes
  and manufactured home communities.
Title 4 – Accessing the American Dream
Sec. 401 – Creating Incentives for Small Dollar Loan Originators
   Directs the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) to study and report on
  mortgage loan originator compensation practices and their impact on the availability of
  small dollar mortgages (loans of $100,000 or less).
   Enables the CFPB to issue regulations ensuring fair compensation for these loans.
Sec. 402 – Small Dollar Mortgage Points and Fees
   Requires the CFPB to evaluate the impact of current points and fees thresholds on small
  dollar mortgage lending and authorizes the agency to adjust these limits regulatorily to
  encourage more small dollar mortgage loans.
Sec. 403 – Appraisal Industry Improvement Act
   Reforms appraisal licensing and training, enhances standards for FHA-approved
  appraisers, adds flexibility for trainee appraisers, and authorizes grants to support
  appraisal workforce development.
Sec. 404 – Helping More Families Save Act
   Authorizes HUD to implement a multi-year demonstration project, testing and evaluating
  an opt-out approach to the Family Self-Sufficiency (FSS) program, among other program
  changes.
Sec. 405 – Choice in Affordable Housing Act
   Aims to reduce delays in HUD inspections by allowing units financed through certain
  federal housing programs—the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), the HOME
  Program, and the Department of Agriculture (USDA) Rural Housing Service—to
  automatically meet Housing Choice Voucher (HCV) inspection requirements if they have
  passed an inspection within the past year.
     Allows new landlords to request advance inspections, helping to expand housing options
  for voucher holders and incentivizing greater landlord participation in the HCV program.
Title 5 – Program Reform
Sec. 501 – Reforming Disaster Recovery Act
   Permanently authorizes and reforms HUD’s Community Development Block Grant
  Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) program to better address the needs of low- to moderate-
  income households following major disasters.
Sec. 502 – HOME Investment Partnerships Reauthorization and Improvement Act
   Reauthorizes the HOME Investment Partnerships Program.
   Makes administrative revisions and reforms to support housing production.
Sec. 503 – Rural Housing Service Reform Act*
   Makes changes to the USDA’s Rural Housing Service programs, including decoupling
  rental assistance from maturing mortgages, permanently establishing the Housing
  Preservation and Revitalization program for multifamily rental housing, and providing
  funding for technology improvements and increased staff capacity.
Sec. 504 – New Moving to Work Cohort
   Authorizes a new Moving to Work program cohort, Economic Opportunity and Pathways
  to Independence, with specific eligibility and reporting requirements.
Sec. 505 – Reducing Homelessness Through Program Reform Act
   Proposes reforms to federal homelessness programs to increase funding consistency,
  streamline lease-up processes, improve coordination among agencies, and strengthen data
  collection and coordination.
Sec. 506 – Incentivizing Local Solutions to Homelessness
   Allows Emergency Solutions Grant funding recipients to request a waiver of the statutory
  60% spending cap on emergency shelter beds and street outreach.
Title 6 – Veterans and Housing
Sec. 601 – VA Home Loan Awareness Act*
   Adds a disclosure to the Uniform Residential Loan Application informing applicants they
  may be eligible for a Veterans Affairs (VA) Home Loan to increase awareness of and
  access to the program.
Sec. 602 – Veterans Affairs Loan Informed Disclosure (VALID) Act
   Enhances FHA mortgage disclosures to help borrowers compare VA loan options
  alongside conventional and FHA loans.
Sec. 603 – Housing Unhoused Disabled Veterans Act
   Excludes disability benefits received by veterans for the purpose of determining income
  eligibility for the HUD-VASH program.
Title 7 – Oversight and Accountability
Sec. 701 – Requiring Annual Testimony and Oversight from Housing Regulators
   Requires annual testimony from the heads of HUD, FHA, Ginnie Mae, USDA, Federal
  Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), and the VA relating to the status of federal housing
  programs and government-backed mortgages, to enhance oversight and accountability.
Sec. 702 – FHA Reporting Requirements on Safety and Soundness
   Requires that HUD provide monthly reports to Congress relating to the Mutual Mortgage
  Insurance Fund’s statutorily required 2% capital ratio and notify Congress if the fund
  falls below the mandated ratio.
Sec. 703 – United States Interagency Council on Homelessness (USICH) Oversight
     Requires that the USICH include a progress update on its efforts to reduce homelessness
  as part of its annual planning process and that it provides annual testimony to Congress.
Sec. 704 – NeighborWorks Accountability Act
   Establishes an Office of the Inspector General within NeighborWorks America.
Sec. 705 – Appraisal Modernization Act
   Requires mortgage lenders to establish standardized policies to ensure consistent
  treatment of consumers who request a second appraisal.
   Requires the Government Accountability Office to issue a report assessing the feasibility
  of creating a public appraisal database consolidating data collected by the FHFA, HUD,
  USDA, and the VA.
Title 8 – Coordination, Studies, & Reporting
Sec. 801 – HUD-USDA-VA Interagency Coordination Act
   Directs HUD, USDA, and the VA to share information and identify opportunities for
  collaboration to streamline the implementation of their housing programs.
Sec. 802 – Streamlining Rural Housing Act
   Directs HUD and USDA to conduct joint environmental reviews for housing projects
  receiving funding from both agencies.
Sec. 803 – Improving Self-Sufficiency of Families in HUD-Subsidized Housing
   Directs HUD to study the benefits and challenges of work requirements on PHAs
  participating in the Moving to Work demonstration and assisted households.
   S. 1461, the Safe SHORES Act, which would reauthorize HUD’s Recovery Housing
  Program, increase its annual funding, and allow grantees to cover more costs associated
  with providing housing.
   S. 885, the Strategy and Investment in Rural Housing Preservation Act, which would
  strengthen USDA’s Section 515 loan program by allowing for the restructuring of
  existing loans, extending incentives for property owners to remain in the program, and
  providing resources for necessary repairs and restorations while ensuring residents
  continue to receive rental assistance.
   S. 138, the VA Home Loan Awareness Act, which would require mortgage applications
  to inform veterans and surviving spouses that they may be eligible for a VA home loan,
  aiming to boost awareness and use of this underutilized benefit.
   S. 127, the Whole-Home Repairs Act, which would create a national five-year pilot
  program within HUD to allow low- and moderate-income homeowners and small
  landlords to apply for grants and loans to make needed repairs to homes.

SUPPORT

The ROAD to Housing Act has support from a myriad of housing stakeholders including:

US Conference of Mayors
National League of Cities
National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders
National Housing Conference
National Alliance to End Homelessness
Coalition for Affordable Homeownership
Veterans Association of Real Estate Professionals
 AARP
National Association of Realtors
Real Estate Roundtable
Mortgage Bankers Association
National Association of Home Builders
National Apartment Association
National Multifamily Housing Council
Bipartisan Policy Center
Appraisal Institute

OPPOSITION

There does not appear to be any opposition from housing stakeholders or other private sector
entities, for that matter.

FROM:  Jamie Jones

DATE:  November 12, 2025
RE:  S.2293/H.R.4397 – The Muslim Brotherhood Terrorist Designation Act

Senator Ted Cruz, Chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee on Africa and Global
Health Policy, introduced S.2293, the Muslim Brotherhood Terrorist Designation Act, on July 15,
2025. The bill directs the President and Secretary of State to use their statutory authority to
sanction the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist organization. The U.S. has officially listed
individual members, branches (including Hamas), and charities of the Muslim Brotherhood as
terrorists, but has not designated the organization as a whole. S.2293 mandates the Secretary of
State to catalog the MB branches designated as terrorist groups and designate additional ones that
meet relevant criteria, and mandates the designation of the global MB for its support of those
terrorist groups.

There are broadly three ‘ways’ of designating terrorist groups under U.S. statute and authorities:
Congressional designation under the Anti-Terrorism Act of 1987 (ATA), State Dept. designation
as a Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO) pursuant to the Immigration and Nationality Act, and
Treasury Dept. designation as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT) under Executive
Order (EO) 13224. This bill does all three.
    Section 2: Designation of the Muslim Brotherhood under the Anti-Terrorism Act. The
  designation creates a primary embargo, in which Americans are banned from conducting
  transactions on behalf of the group.
    Section 3: Designation of the global Muslim Brotherhood and any Muslim Brotherhood
  branches found to be conducting terrorism pursuant to the Foreign Terrorist Organization
  and the Specially Designated Global Terrorist authorities, implemented through a periodic
  report.
 According to the sponsors of the bill, the Muslim Brotherhood is a transnational Islamist
organization and functions as a global organization, providing material support to Muslim
Brotherhood branches in countries and territories by providing political support, financial
resources, training, services, expert advice, and communications assistance. The MB has sought
to destabilize and undermine United States allies and partners throughout the Middle East,
including in Bahrain, Egypt, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates and has been
outlawed as a terrorist group by the governments of those countries.

S.2293 has been referred to the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations and has been cosponsored
by Senators Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), John Boozman (R-Ark.), Rick Scott (R-Fla.), Ashley Moody
(R-Fla.), and Dave McCormick (R-Pa.).Companion legislation, H.R. 4397, was introduced in the
House by Representatives Mario Díaz-Balart (R-FL) and Jared Moskowitz (D-FL), Co-Chairs of
the Friends of Egypt Caucus. The bill has 19 cosponsors and has been referred to the House
Foreign Affairs Committee and the Judiciary Committee.

SUPPORT

The bill is supported by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD) Action, Christians
United for Israel Action Fund, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), and the
Republican Jewish Coalition.

DATE:  November 12, 2025
RE:  H.R. 3883 – The Muslim Brotherhood is a Terrorist Organization Act of 2025

Representative Nancy Mace (R-SC) introduced H.R. 3883, the Muslim Brotherhood is a Terrorist
Organization Act of 2025, on June 10. The bill has been referred to the House Judiciary
Committee.

The thread bare bill contains two sections: Section 1 covers the bill title; and Section 2 directs the
Secretary of State to formally designate the Muslim Brotherhood as a foreign terrorist organization
pursuant to Section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 USC 1189). The bill contains
no explanatory statement. According to Congresswoman Mace, the Muslim Brotherhood doesn’t
just support terrorism, it inspires it. Mace, in introducing the bill, said “President Trump was right
when he said the Muslim Brotherhood is a threat to global security, and it’s long past time we call
them what they are: terrorists.”

According the Representative Mace, H.R. 3883 activates critical national security tools including
financial sanctions, asset freezes, travel bans, and targeted law enforcement, to dismantle the
group’s operations in the U.S. and abroad. Mace states that the Muslim Brotherhood has
historically been linked to radical Islamist movements, with affiliates fueling terrorism and
undermining key U.S. allies.

It should be noted that Representative Nancy Mace is campaigning for Governor of South Carolina
and will not be returning as a member of Congress following the mid-term elections.
Representative Mace’s bill is unlikely to be considered by the Judiciary Committee in this
Congress.

TO:  Mandy Jiang, Senior Management Analyst
  City of Beverly Hills

FROM:  Jamie Jones
  Jamie.jones@davidturch.com
  202-543-3744

DATE:  November 12, 2025
RE:  H.R. 1267 – Water System PFAS Liability Protection Act

Representative Maria Gluesenkamp Perez (D-WA) and Representative Cleste Maloy (R-UT)
introduced H.R. 1267, the Water System PFAS Liability Protection Act, on February 12. The bill
exempts public water agencies from liability under the Comprehensive Environmental Response,
Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 with respect to releases of PFAS (perfluoroalkyl and
polyfluoroalkyl) substances. The bill is aimed at protecting water utilities, who are passive
receivers of PFAS, from financial and legal liabilities associated with decades of use of these
chemicals in manufacturing and consumer products.

Last year, the EPA formally designate two of the most common PFAS chemicals –
Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) – as hazardous
substances under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act
(CERCLA), federal statute dealing with superfund cleanup. This designation could put drinking
water utilities at risk of incurring cleanup liability when they take necessary steps to remove and
dispose of PFAS deposited into water supplies by upstream polluting industries. In addition,
wastewater and stormwater utilities could also be put at risk as they receive PFAS chemicals
through the raw influent that arrives at the treatment plant or through municipal stormwater runoff.

While EPA has announced an “enforcement discretion” policy that intends to focus on polluters
that are responsible for the contamination and have profited from PFAS, such a policy is viewed
by water industry stakeholders as insufficient to ensure that drinking water and clean water
ratepayers will be permanently protected from CERCLA legal defense costs and cleanup liability
for PFAS. Water agencies highlight that not only is the enforcement discretion policy nonbinding
and subject to revision or reversal at any time, but potentially responsible parties have already
publicly indicated that they will use every legal means available to require public agencies to pay
 for PFAS cleanups. CERCLA provides an opportunity for manufacturers and users of PFAS to
defray their own cost burden, brought on by their own actions, by forcing communities around the
country into litigation. These communities are often those that have been the most impacted by
PFAS pollution and are therefore the least able to afford such costs. While EPA’s enforcement
discretion policy is well intentioned, the Agency simply cannot provide the protection that water
utilities and their ratepayers need.

BACKGROUND

Without congressional action, water and wastewater utilities and their customers will be at risk of
incurring the significant cost of cleaning up PFAS contaminated sites. Drinking water and
wastewater utilities face this risk because they passively receive these per- and polyfluoroalkyl
substances (PFAS) from upstream polluting industries and PFAS-laden products. After removing
PFAS from water supplies, water utilities possess residuals that contain those PFAS, which must
be disposed of in accordance with applicable law. However, should the disposal site ever become
subject to a Superfund cleanup, the water system could be treated as a PFAS polluter – and be
responsible for a portion or even all the cleanup costs – forcing local ratepayers to cover the bill
after they already paid to remove the contaminants from their source water. Wastewater and
stormwater utilities would face similar liability through no fault of their own because they either
receive PFAS chemicals through the raw influent that arrives at the treatment plant or through the
municipal stormwater runoff that they manage. These flows can come from domestic, industrial,
and commercial sources and may contain PFAS constituents ranging from trace to higher
concentrations, depending on the nature of the dischargers to the sewer or stormwater system.
These flows are not generated by the utility; rather, the utility provides the critical human health
and environmental service of managing and treating this influent to meet all the requirements of
the Clean Water Act. Congressional action is necessary to distinguish these utilities from the
entities responsible for introducing PFAS into the environment.

SUPPORT

American Water Works Association, Association of Metropolitan Water Agencies, National
Association of Clean Water Agencies, National Association of Water Companies, National Rural
Water Association and Water Environment Federation

The City’s Legislative Platform is updated annually, identifying positions on key legislative
priorities for the upcoming legislative session. As part of this process, the Legislative / Lobby
Committee reviews the proposed amendments to the upcoming year’s Legislative Platform. Once
approved, the recommended amendments to the Legislative Platform will be taken to a Study
Session for City Council consideration, then adopted under consent at a later City Council formal
meeting.

The Platform’s legislative priorities are established to encompass City Council’s objectives in the
interest of the City. Priorities are listed by category and significance, ranging from Local Control
to Utilities. The objective of the Legislative Platform is to outline the City’s policy statements on
various legislative matters and serve as foundation for the City to support or oppose local, state,
and federal legislation. The upcoming 2026 legislative session is the final year of the two-year
legislative cycle and is characterized by a fast moving, deadline-driven pace.

Platform Overview
The purpose of the legislative platform is to provide a means for summarizing the City’s
core legislative principles for the purpose of advocacy efforts at the regional, state, and
federal levels. The Legislative Platform contains broad policy statements pertaining to a
variety of issues that impact the City of Beverly Hills.

The legislative platform sets forth the City’s legislative objectives for the 2025 legislative
session and provides direction for our legislative advocates as they work to secure clear
and strategic initiatives in Sacramento and Washington, D.C. Approval of the legislative
platform also streamlines the City’s process and allows the City’s Executive team to
effectively respond and take immediate action on pressing legislation under City Council
direction.

The policies established within the platform do not preclude City Council consideration of
additional legislative matters arising throughout the year that may be brought forward for
City Council action, as presented to the City Council Legislative/Lobby Liaison
Committee.

Re:  CHP Evaluation of SAEDs Pursuant to SB 1079 (Portantino), 2022

On September 19, 2022, Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 1079 (Portantino), Chapter
449, Statutes of 2022 into law, directing the California Highway Patrol (CHP) to conduct a
study to evaluate Sound-Activated Enforcement Devices (SAEDs) as a monitoring and
enforcement tool for excessive exhaust noise.

The purpose of the study was for the CHP to assess the efficacy of SAEDs and to determine
their ability to capture exhaust noise violations to the degree that the information would
allow for enforcement action. This study was a collaborative management effort between
the CHP and the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans).

CHP staff within their Research and Planning Section collaborated with staff Caltrans to
identify locations on the state highway system and install the devices in coordination with
the respective vendors. The analysis of the data and compilation of this report was
performed by the CHP’s Commercial Vehicle Section.

The goal of the study was to determine the efficacy of emergent technology as a tool for
monitoring vehicle exhaust noise and enforcing applicable laws. The CHP evaluated the
capability of SAEDs from three different companies to accurately identify vehicles
producing exhaust noise beyond the allowable sound limits specified in the California
Vehicle Code (CVC). After conducting thorough market research, SAEDs from the following
three companies were selected for this study:
     TNL,
    Intelligent Instruments, and
    Jenoptik (through its subsidiary, Traffipax).

The SAEDs were installed throughout the greater Sacramento area.

TNL
TNL’s SAED was installed on the westbound United States (US) Highway 50 on-ramp from
northbound Sunrise Boulevard. Installation was completed by the California Department
of Transportation (Caltrans) on December 21, 2023. However, the data available through
TNL’s web-based interface was largely unsuitable for manual review. As a result, a
thorough analysis of individual events could not be conducted.

Intelligent Instruments
Intelligent Instruments’ SAED was installed on the westbound US-50 on-ramp from
southbound Watt Avenue. Installation was completed by Caltrans on February 3, 2024. A
total of 328 events from February 9, 2024, to March 27, 2024, were analyzed as part of this
study.

Jenoptik
Jenoptik’s SAED was installed on the westbound Interstate (I) Highway 80 on-ramp from
southbound Elkhorn Boulevard. Installation was completed by Caltrans on February 28,
2024. Jenoptik encountered technical issues after installation and was unable to provide
any data for CHP review prior to the completion of this report.

Study Findings
Of the three SAEDs installed, only Intelligent Instruments’ SAED generated data which
could be analyzed by CHP on a web-based interface. However, all SAEDs evaluated were
determined to be inadequate as a standalone enforcement tool and unsatisfactory in their
ability to identify individual offending vehicles to the degree necessary for enforcement
action.

Recommendation
Based on the results of the study, the CHP does not recommend the use of SAEDs as a
standalone enforcement tool to be used as the sole basis for issuing citations for exhaust
noise violations.
